messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya, a 33-year-old graphic designer, first sought help after months of living as though she were still being watched. The stalking had begun with a man she had briefly spoken to after a neighborhood event, and what made it terrifying was not any single dramatic confrontation but the way he seemed to materialize in ordinary places: outside her apartment building, near the café where she worked on her laptop, and once beside her on the bike path when she was commuting home. The sight of a bicycle now pulled her back to that stretch of path and the knowledge of being shadowed from behind; when someone walked too close behind her, or a cyclist slowed near her, her body reacted before she could think. She would feel a surge of danger in her chest, certain that something was about to happen even when nothing was obviously wrong. In those moments she became convinced that the world was a dangerous place and that people were not what they seemed. She had come to believe that the people responsible had faced no consequences, which made the threat feel ongoing rather than over. That belief sharpened the way she read every glance and footstep, and the more she felt herself being watched, the more the old fear returned.

Over time Maya’s days narrowed around that fear. At work, if she had to leave the design studio to meet a client or pick up lunch, she would automatically scan reflections in shop windows and check who was behind her. She made sure to stay near an exit in cafés and meeting spaces, and before she felt comfortable anywhere she always identified escape routes. She avoided going anywhere near the street where the stalking had been most intense, even when it was the quickest route home, because simply being there made her feel as if she had invited danger back into her life. These precautions gave her brief relief, but they also kept the whole episode vivid and close. Each time she mapped exits or watched the door instead of her laptop screen, she was reminded again that she did not feel safe. That constant vigilance fed her conviction that the world was dangerous and that others could not be trusted, and it left her more alert to any sign of being followed. The more she scanned, the more often she noticed a figure walking at the same pace or a cyclist lingering nearby, and those moments immediately triggered the sense that she was under threat again.

Maya began to notice that her own coping style was keeping the fear alive. Because she avoided the street where it happened, she never had the chance to see it as ordinary again; every detour made the place feel more loaded, more like proof that something terrible had occurred there. Her habit of staying close to exits and plotting escape routes also kept her attention fixed on danger, which made her jumpy and easily startled. A coworker appearing suddenly at her desk or a bike bell ringing behind her could send a jolt through her whole body, as if she had been caught off guard by something far worse. Those alarm reactions made her even more certain that she was not overreacting but correctly sensing danger, and that certainty pushed her back into the same routines of checking and avoiding. In turn, the more she lived that way, the more she felt the world was unsafe and other people were not what they seemed.

By the time she came to therapy, Maya and her husband had started planning errands around where she could park, walk, and leave quickly. She had nearly stopped riding her bicycle, though it had once been her favorite way to get around the city. She found herself declining invitations if they involved crowded sidewalks, unfamiliar neighborhoods, or any situation where she would have to turn her back on people. At work she was still functioning, but she was exhausted by how much of her attention went to watching doors, mirrors, and approaching footsteps instead of her designs. What finally brought her in was a recent evening when she left the office late, saw a cyclist slowing beside her, and felt her heart lurch as if the stalking had resumed; she knew then that she could not keep arranging her life around escape routes and constant scanning. Maya said she wanted to believe the danger belonged to the past, but what frightened her most was the sense that it never truly had.
